extraction_notes.note: Definitions 8 and 9 use a custom `customdef` environment that latex_facts does not report; they were extracted as prose definition nodes (confidence 0.95), and \ref{def:sensi:para} resolves to a section label, so its edges were added as term edges.
The Section 5 proof sketches carry rigor semi_formal and alternative proves edges, as the proof-sketch rule says, although the rigor rule excludes proofs; the finishing step warns about this.

The sketches cite lemmas that are stated inside later proofs (e.g. Lemmas 13-15 in the proof of Proposition 5). These refs describe where the lemmas are used, so they are marked as mentions. Equation (46), which restates the definition of sigma^2(chi*) inside the proof of Theorem 3, is a mention edge into Proposition 4. Without these marks the checker reports spurious cycles.

Theorem 1 (a-d) and Corollary 1 (a-c) are proved part by part in separate subsections, so each part is a claim nested in its result. Item labels resolve to the parent result, so the refs 'This proves Theorem 1-a' were added as mention edges.
The prose proofs of Propositions 1 and 2 contain the statements of Lemmas 4-7, whose proofs are in the appendix. Proposition 2's proof has no closing sentence, so it ends with Lemma 7.
Remark 4 (h(f) >= 1, with its argument) and Remark 3 (range of mu) assert small results. They were kept as remarks because they mix assertion, proof and discussion.

Not extracted: the abstract and the introduction's contribution bullets (informal O-notation summaries of Theorems 1-3 and Corollaries 1-2), the notation table in Section 5 (it is the only place gamma(.) is introduced outside Lemma 11), and the simulation figures.

Notation introduced inside whole-section proofs (X, Y, Z in Section 7; vartheta, eta in Section 8; P(d-hat,zeta), Delta(d-hat,zeta) in Section 22) is kept as proof steps under step rule 4, even though Algorithms 1-2 use the Section 22 symbols.

nodes.name: Threshold test functions (Damaschke)
nodes.statement: For example, Damaschke~\cite{damaschke2006threshold} considered {\it threshold test functions}: the test outcome is negative if the number of defectives in a test is no larger than the lower threshold $\ell$; positive if no smaller than the upper threshold $u$; and arbitrary (negative or positive) otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Test outcome negative if at most $\ell$ defectives, positive if at least $u$, arbitrary in between.

nodes.name: Number of items n and defectives d (introduction)
nodes.statement: Let $n$ and $d$ be the number of all items and the number of defective items, respectively.

nodes.name: Damaschke's adaptive threshold group-testing algorithm
nodes.statement: For $u=\ell+1$,~\cite{damaschke2006threshold} proposed an adaptive algorithm with the number of tests scaling as ${\cal O}\left( (d+u^2) \log n\right)$ to exactly identify the defectives.
nodes.statement_short: For $u=\ell+1$ an adaptive algorithm identifies the defectives exactly with $O((d+u^2)\log n)$ tests.
conclusions: proposed an adaptive algorithm with the number of tests scaling as ${\cal O}\left( (d+u^2) \log n\right)$ to exactly identify the defectives

nodes.name: Damaschke's impossibility and approximate recovery for gapped thresholds
nodes.statement: However, for $u>\ell+1$, they proved that the defectives cannot be exactly identified, but ${\cal O}\left( (dn^b+d^u) \log n\right)$ adaptive tests suffice to identify the defectives if up to $(u-1)(1+\frac{1}{b})-\ell$ misidentifications are allowed (here $b>0$ is an arbitrary constant).
nodes.statement_short: For $u>\ell+1$ exact identification is impossible; $O((dn^b+d^u)\log n)$ adaptive tests suffice with bounded misidentifications.

nodes.name: Chen-Fu non-adaptive threshold group testing
nodes.statement: Chen and Fu \cite{chen2009nonadaptive} proposed a non-adaptive algorithm for which the number of tests scales as ${\cal O}\left( \sigma d^{u+1} \log (\frac n d)\right)$ if up to $u-\ell-1$ misidentifications and $\sigma$ erroneous tests are allowed.
nodes.statement_short: Non-adaptive threshold group testing with $O(\sigma d^{u+1}\log(n/d))$ tests allowing misidentifications and erroneous tests.

nodes.name: Cheraghchi's improved non-adaptive threshold bound
nodes.statement: Subsequently, Cheraghchi \cite{cheraghchi2010improved} showed that it can be reduced to ${\cal O}\left( d^{u-\ell+1} \log d \log (\frac n d)\right)$.

nodes.name: Threshold group testing with d^{3/2} tests
nodes.statement: More recently, for the special case $u=\ell+1$, \cite{de2020} reduced it further to ${\cal O}\left( d^{\frac 3 2}  \log (\frac n d)\right)$ when $u$ is asymptotically close to $\frac d 2$.

nodes.name: Bernoulli gap stochasticity
nodes.statement: For Bernoulli gap stochasticity, the test outcome is equally likely to be negative or positive whenever the number of defectives in a test is in the interval $(\ell, u)$.

nodes.name: Linear gap stochasticity
nodes.statement: For linear gap stochasticity, the probability of having positive outcome increases linearly as the number of defectives ranges from $\ell$ to $u$.

nodes.name: Chan et al. stochastic threshold group-testing bounds
nodes.statement: By allowing a small error probability $\varepsilon$, they proposed a two-stage adaptive algorithm with $11.09e^2d \log n +{\cal O}\left(d\log( \frac{1} {\varepsilon})\right)$ number of tests and a non-adaptive algorithm with ${\cal O}\left(\log(\frac {1} {\varepsilon})d\sqrt{\ell}\log n\right)$ number of tests for Bernoulli gap stochasticity, and a non-adaptive algorithm with ${\cal O}\left((u-\ell-1)^2d\log n\right)+{\cal O}\left(d\log(\frac {1} {\varepsilon})\right)$ number of tests for linear gap stochasticity.
nodes.statement_short: Adaptive and non-adaptive test counts for Bernoulli-gap and linear-gap stochastic threshold group testing.

nodes.name: Reisizadeh et al. improvement for Bernoulli gap stochasticity
nodes.statement: Recently,  for Bernoulli gap stochasticity,  Reisizadeh {\it et al.} \cite{reisizadeh2018} improved the number of tests required to ${\cal O}\left(\sqrt{u}d\log ^3 n \right)$.

nodes.name: Items, defective set and non-defective items
nodes.statement: A set $\mathcal{N}:=\{1,\dots, n\}$ of $n$ items contains a subset $\mathcal{D}\subsetneq \mathcal{N}$ of  \textit{defective} items -- elements in $\mathcal{N}\setminus \mathcal{D}$ are called \textit{non-defective}.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{N}=\{1,..,n\}$ items; $\mathcal{D}$ the defective subset; the rest are non-defective.

nodes.name: Combinatorial group testing model
nodes.statement: We follow the ``combinatorial group testing model'', which assumes that the size of defective set ${\cal D}$ is fixed as $d$, and each such subset has the same probability.

nodes.name: Number of defectives known a priori
nodes.statement: In this work we assume that the {\it number} $d = |{{\cal D}}|$ of defectives is known {\it a priori}.

nodes.name: Measurement (test) function f
nodes.statement: Our primary contribution in this work is  to consider a very general class of (probabilistic) measurement functions  $f(\cdot): \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \rightarrow [0, 1]$. The input, say $x$, to the measurement function $f(x)$ is the number of defective items $x$ in a given pool, and the value of $f(x)$ is the probability that the given test results in a positive test outcome.
nodes.statement_short: $f(x)\in[0,1]$ is the probability a pool with $x$ defectives tests positive.

nodes.name: Dependence of f on d
nodes.statement: A slight notational subtlety here -- since we will be interested in asymptotic results (when $d$ and $n$ are ``large"), in the interest of generality we allow the function $f(\cdot)$ to also depend on the value of $d$, the overall number of defectives in the population of size $n$. Hence our notation $f(\cdot)$ actually indexes a set $\{f_d(\cdot)\}_{d}$ of measurement functions. Since we assume the number $d$ to be known in advance (see the discussion above, and Footnote~\ref{fn:est-def}) thus the actual function $f_d(\cdot)$ in the set $f(\cdot)$ is well-specified. Thus for notational convenience we suppress the dependence of $f(\cdot)$ on $d$ in the remainder of this paper. Hence a statement like $f(0) \xrightarrow{d\rightarrow \infty}0$ should be interpreted as meaning that $\lim_{d \rightarrow \infty} f_d(0) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ stands for a family $\{f_d\}$; asymptotic statements like $f(0)\to0$ are limits in $d$.

nodes.name: Monotone measurement functions
nodes.statement: In this work we restrict ourselves to the natural class of measurement, {\it monotone} measurement functions, i.e., $x\geq y \Rightarrow f(x)\geq f(y)$.

nodes.name: Classical group testing as a special case
Equation (1)
nodes.label: f(x)_classical

nodes.name: Linear gap stochastic group testing as a special case
Equation (2)
nodes.statement:
f(x)= 
    \left\{
    \begin{array}{cc}
    0     & \; x \leq \ell, \\
    \frac{x-\ell}{u-\ell}     &  \; \ell < x< u,\\
    1   & \; x \geq u,

nodes.label: f(x)_linear_gap

nodes.name: Non-triviality assumption f(0)<f(d)
nodes.statement: To avoid triviality, we further assume that $f(0)<f(d)$. (If $f(0)=f(d)$, no sequence of tests can ever reliably recover the defective set ${\cal D}$.)

nodes.name: Noisy test function
nodes.statement: If $0 < f(0) < f(d) < 1$,  we say that $f(\cdot)$ is {\it noisy}.

nodes.name: Classical noisy group-testing test functions
Equation (3)
nodes.label: f(x)_classical_noisy

nodes.name: One-sided near-noiseless test function
nodes.statement: If either $ f(0) \xrightarrow{d\rightarrow \infty} 0$ or $f(d) \xrightarrow{d\rightarrow \infty} 1$  we say that $f(\cdot)$ is {\it one-sided near-noiseless}, and

nodes.name: Near-noiseless test function
nodes.statement: If both $ f(0) \xrightarrow{d\rightarrow \infty} 0$ and $f(d) \xrightarrow{d\rightarrow \infty} 1$ hold we say that $f(\cdot)$ is {\it near-noiseless}.

nodes.name: One-sided noiseless test function
nodes.statement: Analogously, if either $ f(0) = 0$ or $f(d) = 1$ we say that $f(\cdot)$ is {\it one-sided noiseless}, and

nodes.name: Noiseless test function
nodes.statement: If both $ f(0) = 0$ and $f(d) = 1$ hold we say that $f(\cdot)$ is {\it noiseless}.

nodes.name: Adaptive and non-adaptive group testing
nodes.statement: Group testing schemes can be adaptive (where each test may be designed based on the outcomes of all preceding tests) or non-adaptive (where all tests must be chosen prior to observing any test outcomes).

nodes.name: Test matrix M
nodes.statement: Non-adaptive generalized group-testing test designs are specified by a (possibly randomly chosen) binary matrix $\boldsymbol{M}\in\{0,1\}^{T\times n}$, where $M_{ji} = 1$ if test $j$ includes item $i$ and $M_{ji} = 0$ otherwise.

nodes.name: Probability of error
nodes.statement:
The probability of error of any non-adaptive algorithm (with a specified test matrix $\boldsymbol{M}$) is defined as the probability 
that the estimated defective set $\hat{\mathcal{D}}$ differs from the true $\mathcal{D}$. 
This probability is over the elements comprising ${\cal D}$ (which is assumed to be distributed uniformly at random from all $d$-sized subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$), over the randomness in test outcomes (since each test with $x$ defectives may result in a positive test outcome with probability $f(x)$ and a negative test outcome with probability $1-f(x)$), and randomness if any in the decoding rule.
nodes.statement_short: Probability that the estimated defective set differs from the true one, over $\mathcal{D}$, test noise and decoder randomness.

nodes.name: (1-epsilon)-reliable test design
nodes.statement: We require that the probability of error is bounded from above by some $\varepsilon$. That is,  $\Pr(\hat{\mathcal{D}}\neq \mathcal{D})\leq \varepsilon$ -- such test designs will be called $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable.

nodes.name: Bernoulli test design
nodes.statement: We consider Bernoulli designs -- see, for example, \cite{AtiaS12,ScarlettC16,ScarlettC17,Aldridge17,Monograph19}. That is, the test matrix ${\boldsymbol{M}}$ is a ${T} \times n$ binary matrix in which each entry is independently chosen to equal $1$ with probability ${q}$ and $0$ otherwise, for some design parameters $T$ and ${q}\in (0,1)$ to be specified later.
differentia: each entry is independently chosen to equal $1$ with probability ${q}$

nodes.name: Choice between the two decoding rules
nodes.statement: Note that both decoding rules work for all ${q} \in (0,1)$. However, as we will elaborate in Section \ref{sec:proof_thm_1_1} that, the first rule requires fewer tests for $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable recovery when ${q} \in (0,1/2]$, whereas the second rule requires fewer tests for $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable recovery when ${q} \in (1/2,1)$. Hence we use decoding rule $1$ if ${q}\leq \frac 1 2$, and  decoding rule $2$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Use decoding rule 1 when $q\le1/2$ and rule 2 otherwise, since each needs fewer tests in its range.

nodes.name: Decoding Rule 1
nodes.statement_short: Classify item $i$ defective iff the fraction of positive tests among those containing $i$ exceeds $(P(-,q)+P(+,q))/2$.

nodes.name: Count tests containing item i
nodes.statement: More precisely, denote by ${{m}_{i}}$ the number of tests that item $i$ participates in, and denote by ${{m}_{i}^+}$ (respectively ${{m}_{i}^-}$) the number of tests with positive (respectively negative) outcome within these ${{m}_{i}}$ tests.
nodes.statement_short: Count the tests containing item $i$ and their positive/negative outcomes.

nodes.name: Intuition behind the two decoding rules
nodes.statement:
As noted in Section~\ref{sec:test_design}  we use a Bernoulli test design, where each item participates in a test in an i.i.d. manner with probability ${q}$. Both of our two decoding rules, specified in~\eqref{eq:classification_small_q} and~\eqref{eq:classification_large_q}, proceed by classifying each item $i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$ as defective or non-defective independently of any other item.

In particular, Decoding Rule $1$, specified in~\eqref{eq:classification_small_q}, proceeds as follows. For any test including item $i$, we denote by ${P(-,{q})}$ the probability of having a positive outcome if item $i$ is non-defective and by ${P(+,{q})}$ if item $i$ is defective. Due to the monotonicity of our test function $f(\cdot)$, ${P(+,{q})} > {P(-,{q})}$.  By the law of large numbers, when item $i$ participates in a large enough number of tests, the fraction of positive-outcome tests converges to either ${P(-,{q})}$ or ${P(+,{q})}$ depending on whether the item is non-defective or defective respectively. Therefore, decoding rule \eqref{eq:classification_small_q} proceeds by classifying $i$ as defective or not by checking that the fraction of positive test outcomes is closer to ${P(+,{q})}$ or ${P(-,{q})}$. 

Analogously, Decoding Rule 2 specified in~\eqref{eq:classification_large_q} is similar, but now makes use of the tests {\it not} including item $i$, with ${Q(-,{q})}$ denoting the probability of having a positive outcome if item $i$ is non-defective, and ${Q(+,{q})}$ denoting the corresponding probability if item $i$ is defective. As above, due to the monotoncity of $f(\cdot)$, ${Q(-,{q})} > {Q(+,{q})}$. The fraction of positive-outcome tests converges to ${Q(-,{q})}$ and ${Q(+,{q})}$, respectively, and $i$ is classified according to which fraction is closer. 

The reason we have two different decoding rules is since, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:T} when ${q} \in (0,1/2]$,
 the first rule requires fewer tests than the second does for $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable recovery, with the situation reversed in ${q} \in (1/2,1)$.
nodes.statement_short: By the law of large numbers the positive-test fraction concentrates at $P(\pm,q)$ (or $Q(\pm,q)$), so thresholding at the midpoint classifies items.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 2
nodes.statement:
Lemma~\ref{lem:sensi:para:bound}, whose proof can be found in Appendix~\ref{app:sensi:para:bound}, helps provide a universal bound on the the sensitivity parameter for any monotone function $f(\cdot)$.

In order to simplify the $\min\left\{{U}-{L} , \sqrt{{L}+1} , \sqrt{d-{U}+1}\right\}$ term, we first split our analysis into two cases, corresponding to the scenarios $f\left(\left\lceil d/2\right \rceil\right)\geq (f(0)+f(d))/2$ and $f\left(\left\lceil d/2\right \rceil\right) < (f(0)+f(d))/2$ -- we choose ${L}$ and ${U}$ from $[0,d/2]$ or $(d/2,d]$ accordingly. This enables us to argue that only one of $\sqrt{{L}+1}$ and $\sqrt{d-{U}+1}$ is active in the $\min\left\{{U}-{L} , \sqrt{{L}+1} , \sqrt{d-{U}+1}\right\}$ term, simplifying our argumentation. We focus on the first case -- the proof of the second case is analogous. Considering any ${\upsilon} \in (0,1]$ and ${k} = \lceil \log (1/{\upsilon}) + 1 \rceil$, we construct a sequence  $\{{S}_{{i}}\}$ with ${k}+1$ elements such that $\frac{{S}_{{i}+1}^2} {  {S}_{i}+1  } \le 2d^{1+{\upsilon}}$ for all ${i}$. We then argue that there exists two adjacent elements ${S}_{\ell}$ and ${S}_{{\ell}+1}$ such that $f({S}_{{\ell}+1}) - f({S}_{{\ell}}) \ge (f(d)-f(0)) / 2{k}$. Finally, using the definition of ${H(f)}$ in \eqref{eq:def:sensi:para} with ${L}={S}_{{\ell}}$ and ${U}={S}_{{\ell}+1}$ and letting ${\upsilon} = 1/\log d$, one can prove Lemma \ref{lem:sensi:para:bound}.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: split on whether $f(\lceil d/2\rceil)$ is above the midpoint, build a geometric-like sequence $S_i$, and find adjacent points with a large increment.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 1(a)
nodes.statement:
We first collect various inequalities relating quantities such as ${P(+,{q})}$, ${P(-,{q})}$, ${Q(+,{q})}$, ${Q(-,{q})}$, etc, in Lemma~\ref{lem:relation:quantities}, whose proof may be found in Appendix~\ref{app:convert_delta_nabla}. With these relations at hand, the probability of error of these two decoding rules can be analyzed via standard concentration inequalities, collected in Appendix~\ref{app:tail-bound}. 

In particular Proposition~\ref{prop:error_small_q}, posits that for Decoding Rule 1, $T \geq \frac{13}{6{q}}{m}$ tests allow for $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable recovery of the set of ${\cal D}$ of defectives. This is proved in two steps. 
First, in Lemma~\ref{lem:num_tests_lb}, we compute the probability that an arbitrary item participates in less than ${m}$ tests, which, by using the Chernoff bound \cite{chernoff}, is no larger than $\frac{\varepsilon}{2n}$. Second, conditioning on the event that each item participates in at least ${m}$ tests, in Lemma~\ref{lem:num_tests_correctness} we compute the probability of misidentification (either false alarm or missed detection). Using the Chernoff bound, this probability is again no larger than $\frac{\varepsilon}{2n}$. Combining these two parts with a union bound yields Proposition~\ref{prop:error_small_q}. 

Proposition~\ref{prop:error_large_q} similarly analyzes Decoding Rule 2 -- here we show that $T \geq \frac{13}{6(1-{q})} {s}$ tests allow for $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable recovery of the set of ${\cal D}$ of defectives. This is proved in a similar manner to Proposition~\ref{prop:error_small_q}. In Lemma \ref{lem:num_tests_lb_l}, we compute the probability that an arbitrary item participates in more than $T-{s}$ tests is no larger than $\frac{\varepsilon}{2n}$. Then, conditioning on the event that each item participates in at most $T-{s}$ tests, in Lemma \ref{lem:num_tests_correctness_l} we compute the probability of misidentification (either false alarm or missed detection) is again no larger than $\frac{\varepsilon}{2n}$. Taking the union bound over these two parts gives us Proposition \ref{prop:error_large_q}. 

Next, we compare the number of tests required by the two decoding rules. This is accomplished by using the identity ${\nabla({q})} = \frac{{q}}{1-{q}} {\Delta({q})}$ shown in Lemma \ref{lem:relation:quantities}. With this identity, we argue that $T$ tests in \eqref{eq:def:T} suffice.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: Chernoff bounds give per-item participation and misidentification errors at most $\varepsilon/2n$; union bound; compare the two rules via $\nabla=\frac q{1-q}\Delta$.

With these relations at hand, the probability of error of these two decoding rules can be analyzed via standard concentration inequalities, collected in Appendix~\ref{app:tail-bound}.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 1(b)
nodes.statement:
The number of tests chosen in~\eqref{eq:def:T} as $\lceil {{\Gamma}({q})} \rceil$ suffices to ensure $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable recovery, but it is not immediately apparent how this quantity relates to the bound claimed in~\eqref{eq:thm:T:ub}. As a simplifying first step, as noted in the text surrounding~\eqref{eq:def:fTp}, 
instead of bounding ${{\Gamma}({q})}$ directly, we bound instead ${\hat{\Gamma}} ({q}) = \frac{{{\Gamma}({q})}}{{P_{\min}({q})}}$ -- since ${P_{\min}({q})} \leq 1$ (see Lemma~\ref{lem:relation:quantities}) this suffices to give an upper bound on $T$ allowing $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable recovery.

Perhaps the most technically involved part of our work focuses on providing a reasonably tight upper bound -- as accomplished in Proposition~\ref{prop:existence_final} -- on ${\hat{\Gamma}} ({{q}^*})$ in terms of the sensitivity parameter ${H(f)}$ defined in Definition~\ref{def:sensi:para}.

Before discussing Proposition~\ref{prop:existence_final} in the context of general monotone functions, consider first the example of the threshold group-testing function described in~\eqref{eq:threshold:function} (corresponding to negative test outcomes if there are at most ${\ell}$ defectives in a pool).
Intuitively speaking, for accurately classifying each item, we should choose some $q$ such that the gap ${\Delta({q})} ={P(+,{q})}- {P(-,{q})}$ is ``large" (bounded away from $0$). This can also be seen from \eqref{eq:def:fTp}, wherein to minimize ${\hat{\Gamma}} ({q})$, we would like ${\Delta({q})}$ to be as large as possible. 










For the threshold group testing scenario, 
if we choose ${q}={\ell}/d$, then on the one hand if an item $i$ is non-defective the expected number defectives in a pool is ${\ell}$; and on the other hand if item $i$ is defective the expected number of  defectives is $ \frac{{\ell}}{d} (d-1) + 1 \approx {\ell}+1$, and hence the gap ${\Delta({q})}$ in test positivity is about as large as can be hoped for -- one can see that choices of $q$ signficantly larger or smaller than this would result in a smaller gap ${\Delta({q})}$. 

For a general test function $f(\cdot)$, the gap ${\Delta({q})}$ can be regarded as the ``binomially-weighted mean of the increment'' of $f(\cdot)$ (see~\eqref{eq:convert_delta} for the precise expression). To make ${\Delta({q})}$ larger, we should attempt to assign a larger weight to a carefully chosen region ``large-increment-interval'' $[{L},{U}]$ where $f(\cdot)$ exhibits a large increment. 

More precisely, for general test functions $f(\cdot)$ our pathway to proving  Proposition \ref{prop:existence_final} relies on bounding the integral of ${\Delta({q})}$ from ${L}/d$ to $ {U}/d$, which, by the mean value theorem, gives a bound on ${\Delta({q}_0)}$ for some ${q}_0\in [{L}/d,{U}/d]$. To this end in Lemmas~\ref{lem:int_j_alpha}~and~\ref{lem:int_U_L} we provide a delicate saddle-point-approximation style bound for $\int_{{L}/d}^{{U}/d} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} {\,\mathrm{d}} {q}$. This together with Stirling's approximation summarized in Lemma~\ref{lem:stirling} results in Lemma~\ref{lem:existence_pre}, which almost gets us to Proposition \ref{prop:existence_final}, except for two issues.

Firstly, there is a $\frac{ (d-{L}') {U}' }{(d-{U}'){L}'}$ multiplicative term that appears in Lemma~\ref{lem:existence_pre} but not in Proposition \ref{prop:existence_final}. Towards this end, we divide $[{L}',{U}')$ into suitably small intervals $[{{\lambda}_{{i}}},{{\lambda}_{{i}+1}}),\; {i}\in \{0,\dots, {\tau}-1\}$. The intervals are chosen in this manner to satisfy the following two constraints, which are in tension with each other:  
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item In Lemma \ref{lem:exi:alp} -- each ${{\lambda}_{{i}+1}} - {{\lambda}_{{i}}}$ should be larger than $\min\{ {U}'-{L}' , \sqrt{{L}'} , \sqrt{{U}'-{L}'} \}$ that appears in the denominator of Lemma~\ref{lem:existence_pre},
    \item In Lemma \ref{lem:exi:alp_dif} -- each ${{\lambda}_{{i}+1}} - {{\lambda}_{{i}}}$ should  also be small enough so that $\frac{ (d-{{\lambda}_{{i}}}) {{\lambda}_{{i}+1}} }{(d-{{\lambda}_{{i}+1}}){{\lambda}_{{i}}}}$ can be bounded from above by a constant.
\end{enumerate}
 By substituting ${L}' = {{\lambda}_{{\ell}}}$ and ${U}' = {{\lambda}_{{\ell}+1}}$ for a specific ${\ell}$ identified by the mean value theorem in Lemma \ref{lem:exi:slp} allows us to obtain Proposition~\ref{prop:existence}.














Secondly, the ``boundary points", i.e., ${L}=0$ or ${U}=d$, are handled separately in Proposition \ref{prop:existence_margin}.

nodes.name: Reduce to Gamma-hat
nodes.statement:
The number of tests chosen in~\eqref{eq:def:T} as $\lceil {{\Gamma}({q})} \rceil$ suffices to ensure $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable recovery, but it is not immediately apparent how this quantity relates to the bound claimed in~\eqref{eq:thm:T:ub}. As a simplifying first step, as noted in the text surrounding~\eqref{eq:def:fTp}, 
instead of bounding ${{\Gamma}({q})}$ directly, we bound instead ${\hat{\Gamma}} ({q}) = \frac{{{\Gamma}({q})}}{{P_{\min}({q})}}$ -- since ${P_{\min}({q})} \leq 1$ (see Lemma~\ref{lem:relation:quantities}) this suffices to give an upper bound on $T$ allowing $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable recovery.

nodes.name: Key proposition
nodes.statement: Perhaps the most technically involved part of our work focuses on providing a reasonably tight upper bound -- as accomplished in Proposition~\ref{prop:existence_final} -- on ${\hat{\Gamma}} ({{q}^*})$ in terms of the sensitivity parameter ${H(f)}$ defined in Definition~\ref{def:sensi:para}.

nodes.name: Threshold example
nodes.statement:
Before discussing Proposition~\ref{prop:existence_final} in the context of general monotone functions, consider first the example of the threshold group-testing function described in~\eqref{eq:threshold:function} (corresponding to negative test outcomes if there are at most ${\ell}$ defectives in a pool).
Intuitively speaking, for accurately classifying each item, we should choose some $q$ such that the gap ${\Delta({q})} ={P(+,{q})}- {P(-,{q})}$ is ``large" (bounded away from $0$). This can also be seen from \eqref{eq:def:fTp}, wherein to minimize ${\hat{\Gamma}} ({q})$, we would like ${\Delta({q})}$ to be as large as possible.
nodes.statement_short: Motivate a large gap $\Delta(q)$ via the threshold example.

nodes.name: Choice q=l/d
nodes.statement:
For the threshold group testing scenario, 
if we choose ${q}={\ell}/d$, then on the one hand if an item $i$ is non-defective the expected number defectives in a pool is ${\ell}$; and on the other hand if item $i$ is defective the expected number of  defectives is $ \frac{{\ell}}{d} (d-1) + 1 \approx {\ell}+1$, and hence the gap ${\Delta({q})}$ in test positivity is about as large as can be hoped for -- one can see that choices of $q$ signficantly larger or smaller than this would result in a smaller gap ${\Delta({q})}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choosing $q=\ell/d$ nearly maximizes the gap for threshold functions.

nodes.name: Gap as weighted increment
nodes.statement: For a general test function $f(\cdot)$, the gap ${\Delta({q})}$ can be regarded as the ``binomially-weighted mean of the increment'' of $f(\cdot)$ (see~\eqref{eq:convert_delta} for the precise expression). To make ${\Delta({q})}$ larger, we should attempt to assign a larger weight to a carefully chosen region ``large-increment-interval'' $[{L},{U}]$ where $f(\cdot)$ exhibits a large increment.
nodes.statement_short: View $\Delta(q)$ as a binomially weighted mean increment of $f$.

nodes.name: Integral bound
nodes.statement: More precisely, for general test functions $f(\cdot)$ our pathway to proving  Proposition \ref{prop:existence_final} relies on bounding the integral of ${\Delta({q})}$ from ${L}/d$ to $ {U}/d$, which, by the mean value theorem, gives a bound on ${\Delta({q}_0)}$ for some ${q}_0\in [{L}/d,{U}/d]$. To this end in Lemmas~\ref{lem:int_j_alpha}~and~\ref{lem:int_U_L} we provide a delicate saddle-point-approximation style bound for $\int_{{L}/d}^{{U}/d} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} {\,\mathrm{d}} {q}$. This together with Stirling's approximation summarized in Lemma~\ref{lem:stirling} results in Lemma~\ref{lem:existence_pre}, which almost gets us to Proposition \ref{prop:existence_final}, except for two issues.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate $\Delta$ over $[L/d,U/d]$ with saddle-point and Stirling bounds to get Lemma 12.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 1(c)
nodes.statement:
A critical part of our test-design and decoding algorithms is an appropriate choice of ${q} \in (0,1)$. We proceed as follows: we uniformly quantize the interval $(0,1)$ into $\Theta(d^4)$ intervals and calculate the corresponding ${{\Gamma}({q})}$ for each ${q}$, and then set ${q}$ to equal the value ${\hat{{q}}}$ that minimizes ${{\Gamma}({q})}$. We then prove that choosing ${q} = {\hat{{q}}}$ results in our scheme having similar performance to using the value ${q} = {{q}^*}$, i.e., ${\Gamma({\hat{{q}}})} = \Theta({\Gamma} ({{q}^*}))$. 

To this end, in Lemma~\ref{lem:q_range} we first show that ${{q}^*}$ can never be either ``too small" or ``too large" -- i.e., ${{q}^*} \in \left( \frac{1}{376017d^3} , 1-\frac{1}{376017d^3}\right)$. Next, we prove in Lemma~\ref{lem:fT_error} that for all ${\hat{{q}}^*}$ that is close enough to ${{q}^*}$, i.e., $\left|{\hat{{q}}^*} -{{q}^*}\right|\leq \frac{1}{376017d^4}$, we have ${\Gamma({\hat{{q}}^*})}\leq 64e^2{\Gamma} ({{q}^*})$.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: grid-search $q$ over $\Theta(d^4)$ points; Lemma 8 keeps $q^*$ away from 0 and 1 and Lemma 9 shows nearby $q$ lose only a constant factor.

nodes.statement: Since our decoder only needs to count the number of tests and tests with positive outcomes that one item is included in (respectively not included in) and check the ratio via Decoding Rule 1 in \eqref{eq:classification_small_q} (respectively Decoding Rule 2 in \eqref{eq:classification_large_q}), the computational complexity of decoding is ${\cal O}(n T) = {\cal O} \left( n{H(f)} d \log \left( \frac{n}{\varepsilon} \right) \right)$.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 2
nodes.statement:
The proof of our converse argument, which may be found in Section~\ref{sec:proof:converse}, proceeds as follows.
Let $\boldsymbol{{X}}$ be the input vector and $\boldsymbol{{Y}}$ be the outcome vector. We decompose the entropy $H(\boldsymbol{{X}})$ into the conditional entropy term $H(\boldsymbol{{X}}|\boldsymbol{{Y}})$ and the mutual information $I(\boldsymbol{{X}};\boldsymbol{{Y}})$. By the assumption that ${\cal D}$ is uniformly distributed over all $\binom{n}{d}$ size-$d$ subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, we have $H(\boldsymbol{{X}})=\log \binom{n}{d}$. Using Fano's inequality, $H(\boldsymbol{{X}}|\boldsymbol{{Y}})$ can be bounded in terms of the error probability $\varepsilon$. Following techniques similar to the channel coding literature  (see for instance \cite[Sec. 7.3]{yeung08}), one can upper bound ${I}(\boldsymbol{{X}};\boldsymbol{{Y}}) \le \sum_{i=1}^{T} [{H}({Y}_i) - {H}({Y}_i|{Z}_i)]$, where ${{Z}_i}$ denotes the number of defectives in the $i$-th pool. One salient feature of generalized group testing is that the test outcome is no longer deterministic when given the number of defectives in the test pool. That is, ${H}({Y}_i|{Z}_i)>0$ and is not negligible. 

Next (by resorting to an inequality on the $\ln(\cdot)$ function presented in Lemma~\ref{lem:cv:series}) in Lemma \ref{lem:cv_H} we bound each ${H}({Y}_i) - {H}({Y}_i|{Z}_i) \le \frac{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}_i)}{{\mu}({\chi}_i)(1-{\mu}({\chi}_i))}$, where ${\chi}_i$ is the size of the $i$-th pool, ${\mu}({\chi}_i)$ and ${\sigma^{2}}({\chi}_i)$ are, respectively, the mean and variance of being positive. Finally, by optimizing the pool-size parameter ${\chi}$, we prove the lower bound.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: Fano's inequality plus a channel-coding bound on mutual information; each test contributes at most $\sigma^2/(\mu(1-\mu))$; optimize pool size.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: To prove the tightness of our achievability and converse in Theorem~\ref{thm:match} (whose proof may be found in Section~\ref{sec:proof:match}), we show there exists a pair of $({\hat{L}},{\hat{U}})$ such that $\frac{1}{\min\left\{{\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}} , \sqrt{{\hat{L}}+1} , \sqrt{d-{\hat{U}}+1}\right\}}\times \frac{{\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}}}{f({\hat{U}})-f({\hat{L}})} = {\cal O} \left( \frac{1}{\sigma({\chi}^{*})} \right)$. From the definition of ${\chi}^*$ in \eqref{eq:def:optimal-size}, we know that ${\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^*)$ is ``relatively large". This implies that $f(\cdot)$ increases rapidly in the region adjacent to ${\chi}^* \frac{d}{n}$ (which quantity equals the expected number of defectives in the test pool). Therefore it is reasonable to choose ${\chi}^* \frac{d}{n}$ as one of the pair $({\hat{L}},{\hat{U}})$. The existence of the other one is shown in a proof by contradiction in Lemma~\ref{lem:match},  making use of the mean and variance formulae for hypergeometric distributions. Based on Lemma \ref{lem:match}, in Proposition \ref{prop:match} we deal with integrality issues and specify $({\hat{L}},{\hat{U}})$. Finally, invoking  Proposition \ref{prop:existence_final} with this pair of $({\hat{L}},{\hat{U}})$, one can prove Theorem \ref{thm:match}.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: choose $\chi^*d/n$ as one endpoint and find the other by contradiction (Lemma 11), fix integrality (Proposition 4), then apply Proposition 3.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 3
nodes.statement:
Let ${\hat{d}} \geq 2$ be a putative number of defective items. We devise a subroutine which decides whether $d\leq {\hat{d}}-1$ or $d\geq {\hat{d}}$. The idea of the subroutine is similar to that of the algorithm for deciding whether an item is defective or not in Section \ref{sec:test_design}. More precisely, in a Bernoulli test design where items are included with probability ${\zeta}$, denote by ${{P}({\hat{d}},{\zeta})}$ (respectively ${{P}({\hat{d}}-1,{\zeta})}$) 
the probability of having a positive outcome if there are ${\hat{d}}$ (respectively ${\hat{d}}-1$) defectives. By the law of large numbers, when taking a large
enough number of tests, the fraction of positive-outcome tests should be either at least ${{P}({\hat{d}},{\zeta})}$ or at most ${{P}({\hat{d}}-1,{\zeta})}$, depending on whether
there are at least ${\hat{d}}$ defectives or at most ${\hat{d}}-1$ defectives respectively. Therefore, we can reliably estimate whether or not $d$ exceeds ${\hat{d}}$ by checking the fraction of positive test outcomes. By an analogous argument to that of Lemma~\ref{lem:num_tests_correctness}, one can bound the probability of error of the subroutine. 
By a similar argument to the one in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.\ref{thm1:item3}, one can find an upper bound on the number of tests used by the subroutine. Using this subroutine, we can obtain an exact estimate of $d$ via the following two steps.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item To obtain an upper bound on $d$, we perform a sequence of subroutines to check whether $d\leq 2^i$ for $i\in \{1,2, \dots\}$, until the answer is affirmative. 
    \item To find the exact value of $d$, we perform another sequence of subroutines via a binary search.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: a threshold subroutine decides $d<\hat d$ vs $d\ge\hat d$; doubling then binary search find $d$.

nodes.name: Decoding Rule 1
Performance of Decoding Rule 1
nodes.statement:
Suppose that the decoding rule used is \eqref{eq:classification_small_q}. Then we show that the probability of error is at most $ \varepsilon$ 
if 
\begin{equation} {T} \ge {\Gamma}_1({q}) := \frac{13}{6{q}} {m}.
\end{equation}
assumptions: Suppose that the decoding rule used is \eqref{eq:classification_small_q}.
conclusions: the probability of error is at most $ \varepsilon$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement:
This is proved in two steps. 
First, we compute the probability that an arbitrary item participates in less than ${m}$ tests, which can be made sufficiently small. Second, assuming that each item participates in at least ${m}$ tests, we compute the probability of misidentification, which again can be made sufficiently small. Formally, we have the following two lemmas, whose proofs are relegated to Appendices \ref{sec:num_tests_lb} and \ref{sec:num_tests_correctness}, respectively.
\begin{lemma} With probability at least $1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ over the test design, each item $i \in {\cal N}$ participates in at least ${m}$ tests.
\end{lemma}
\begin{lemma} Conditioning on the event that each item participates in at least ${m}$ tests, with probability at least $1-\frac \varepsilon 2$ over the test design, all items are correctly identified using \eqref{eq:classification_small_q}.
\end{lemma}

Upon combining Lemmas \ref{lem:num_tests_lb} and \ref{lem:num_tests_correctness}, via the union bound, the probability that all items are correctly identified is bounded from below by  $1 - \varepsilon$,



which proves Proposition \ref{prop:error_small_q}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemmas 4 and 5 with a union bound.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Thus, for ${q} \leq 1/2$ (respectively ${q} > 1/2$), the number of tests $T$ given in \eqref{eq:def:T} can output the defective set ${\cal D}$ with probability of error at most $\varepsilon$ using the decoding rule \eqref{eq:classification_small_q} (respectively \eqref{eq:classification_large_q}). This proves Theorem \ref{thm:main}-\ref{thm1:item1}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1(b)
nodes.statement:
We provide an explicit bound on the value of ${\hat{\Gamma}} ({q})$ defined in \eqref{eq:def:fTp} for some ${q}$, namely Proposition \ref{prop:existence_final} below, whose proof is presented in Appendix \ref{sec:existence_final}. 
\begin{proposition} There exists some ${q}_0\in(0,1)$ such that
\begin{equation} {\hat{\Gamma}} ({q}_0) \leq 376017 {H(f)} d\log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon } \right),
\end{equation} 
where ${H(f)}$ is the ``sensitivity parameter" defined in \eqref{eq:def:sensi:para}.
\end{proposition}
Combined with \eqref{eq:1>=pmin>max:Delta}, \eqref{eq:def:fTp} and \eqref{eq:def:cpn}, this result yields
\begin{align}
  T=\left\lceil {\Gamma} ({{q}^*}) \right\rceil &= \left \lceil {P_{min}({{q}^*})} {\hat{\Gamma}} ({{q}^*}) \right \rceil \notag\\
  &\leq \left \lceil {P_{min}({{q}^*})} {\hat{\Gamma}} ({q}_0) \right \rceil \notag\\
  &\leq 376017  {P_{min}({{q}^*})}  {H(f)} d\log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon } \right)+1 \\
  &\leq 376017 {H(f)} d\log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon } \right)+1,
\end{align}
which proves Theorem \ref{thm:main}-\ref{thm1:item3}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Proposition 3 with $T=\lceil P_{\min}(q^*)\hat\Gamma(q^*)\rceil$ and minimality of $q^*$.

nodes.name: Proposition 3
Existence of a good design parameter q_0
nodes.statement:
There exists some ${q}_0\in(0,1)$ such that
\begin{equation} {\hat{\Gamma}} ({q}_0) \leq 376017 {H(f)} d\log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon } \right),
\end{equation} 
where ${H(f)}$ is the ``sensitivity parameter" defined in \eqref{eq:def:sensi:para}.
nodes.label: prop:existence_final

nodes.name: Equation (30)
nodes.statement: {\hat{\Gamma}} ({q}_0) \leq 376017 {H(f)} d\log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon } \right),
nodes.label: eq:existence

nodes.name: Chain of bounds
nodes.statement:
Combined with \eqref{eq:1>=pmin>max:Delta}, \eqref{eq:def:fTp} and \eqref{eq:def:cpn}, this result yields
\begin{align}
  T=\left\lceil {\Gamma} ({{q}^*}) \right\rceil &= \left \lceil {P_{min}({{q}^*})} {\hat{\Gamma}} ({{q}^*}) \right \rceil \notag\\
  &\leq \left \lceil {P_{min}({{q}^*})} {\hat{\Gamma}} ({q}_0) \right \rceil \notag\\
  &\leq 376017  {P_{min}({{q}^*})}  {H(f)} d\log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon } \right)+1 \\
  &\leq 376017 {H(f)} d\log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon } \right)+1,
\end{align}
which proves Theorem \ref{thm:main}-\ref{thm1:item3}.

nodes.name: Equation (31)
nodes.statement:
T=\left\lceil {\Gamma} ({{q}^*}) \right\rceil &= \left \lceil {P_{min}({{q}^*})} {\hat{\Gamma}} ({{q}^*}) \right \rceil \notag\\
  &\leq \left \lceil {P_{min}({{q}^*})} {\hat{\Gamma}} ({q}_0) \right \rceil \notag\\

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1(c)
nodes.statement_short: Grid search over $q=j/(376017d^4)$; Lemmas 8 and 9 show the best grid point is within $64e^2$ of optimal; count bit operations.

nodes.name: Lemma 8
q* is bounded away from 0 and 1
nodes.label: lem:q_range

nodes.name: Lemma 9
Stability of Gamma near q*
nodes.label: lem:fT_error

nodes.name: Grid search
nodes.statement: Armed with Lemma \ref{lem:fT_error}, we are now ready to describe our algorithm to selecting ${q}$: First, calculate ${{\Gamma}({q})}$ for all ${q} = \frac{j}{376017 d^4}$, $j = 1,2,\cdots, 376017d^4 - 1$. Then choose the one having the smallest ${{\Gamma}({q})}$ value, denoted by ${\hat{{q}}}$. It follows that ${\Gamma({\hat{{q}}})} \le {\Gamma({\hat{{q}}^*})} \le 64e^2{\Gamma} ({{q}^*})$.
nodes.statement_short: Grid-search $q$ and bound the chosen $\hat q$ via Lemma 9.

nodes.name: Complexity count
nodes.statement: The computational complexity of computing binomial coefficients is ${\cal O}(d^2 \log^2 d)$, and the computational complexity of multiplying the binomial coefficient (which comprises of ${\cal O}(d \log d)$ bits) with ${q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j}$ (which comprises  ${\cal O}(d)$ bits), is ${\cal O}(d^2 \log d)$. According to \eqref{eq:convert_delta}, the computational complexity of computing ${\Delta({q})}$ is ${\cal O}(d^3 \log^2 d)$. Hence the overall computational complexity of this algorithm is ${\cal O} (d^7 \log^2d)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1(d)
nodes.statement: Given the tests and their outcomes, the computational complexity of counting all ${{m}_{i}}$ (respectively ${{s}_{i}}$) and ${{m}_{i}^+}$ (respectively ${{s}_{i}^+}$) is ${\cal O} (nT)$. Thus, the complexity of decoding is ${\cal O}(nT)$. According to Theorem \ref{thm:main}-\ref{thm1:item3}, the complexity is at most ${\cal O} \left(n {H(f)} d\log \left( \frac{n}{\varepsilon} \right) \right)$.

nodes.name: Counting cost
nodes.statement: Given the tests and their outcomes, the computational complexity of counting all ${{m}_{i}}$ (respectively ${{s}_{i}}$) and ${{m}_{i}^+}$ (respectively ${{s}_{i}^+}$) is ${\cal O} (nT)$. Thus, the complexity of decoding is ${\cal O}(nT)$.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 1(b)
nodes.statement: According to Theorem \ref{thm:main}-\ref{thm1:item3}, the complexity is at most ${\cal O} \left(n {H(f)} d\log \left( \frac{n}{\varepsilon} \right) \right)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Fano's inequality and a chain-rule bound $I(X;Y)\le\sum_i[H(Y_i)-H(Y_i|Z_i)]$, each term bounded by Lemma 10, maximized over the pool size.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: In this section, for any given monotone test function $f(\cdot)$, we provide an information-theoretic lower bound on the number of tests required by \emph{any} non-adaptive group testing algorithm that is allowed to make an error with probability at most $\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Goal: lower bound for any non-adaptive scheme.

nodes.name: Notation
nodes.statement:
Let us first introduce some notation which will be used in the proof. We use a binary vector $\boldsymbol{{X}}\in \{0,1\}^n$ to represent the set ${\cal N}$, where $1$s indicate which items are defective.



To estimate $\boldsymbol{{X}}$, we perform $T$ suitable-designed tests, in which each test must be designed prior to observing any outcomes. Let $\boldsymbol{{Z}}=({Z}_1,\dots,{Z}_T)$ be a length $T$ vector, where ${Z}_i$ denotes the number of defectives in the $i$-th test.
The test outcomes are represented by a binary vector $\boldsymbol{{Y}}=({Y}_1,\dots,{Y}_T)\in\{0,1\}^T$, where ${Y}_i=1$ indicates the outcome of the $i$-th test is positive. We emphasize that ${Z}_i$ is independent of $({Y}_1,\dots, {Y}_{i-1},{Y}_{i+1},\dots,{Y}_{T})$. Given the tests and their outcomes, let $\boldsymbol{{\hat{X}}}$ be an estimate of $\boldsymbol{{X}}$.

nodes.name: Entropy decomposition
nodes.statement:
By standard information-theoretic definitions, we have
\begin{align} {H}(\boldsymbol{{X}}) &= {H}(\boldsymbol{{X}}|\boldsymbol{{Y}}) + {I}(\boldsymbol{{X}};\boldsymbol{{Y}})\notag\\
                           &={H}(\boldsymbol{{X}}|\boldsymbol{{Y}},\boldsymbol{{\hat{X}}}) + {I}(\boldsymbol{{X}};\boldsymbol{{Y}})\notag\\
                           &\leq {H}(\boldsymbol{{X}}|\boldsymbol{{\hat{X}}}) + {I}(\boldsymbol{{X}};\boldsymbol{{Y}})
\end{align}
where the second line follows since $\boldsymbol{{\hat{X}}}$ is a function of $\boldsymbol{{Y}}$; the thrid line follows from the fact that conditioning reduces entropy.

nodes.name: Equation (35)
nodes.statement:
{H}(\boldsymbol{{X}}) &= {H}(\boldsymbol{{X}}|\boldsymbol{{Y}}) + {I}(\boldsymbol{{X}};\boldsymbol{{Y}})\notag\\
                           &={H}(\boldsymbol{{X}}|\boldsymbol{{Y}},\boldsymbol{{\hat{X}}}) + {I}(\boldsymbol{{X}};\boldsymbol{{Y}})\notag\\
                           &\leq {H}(\boldsymbol{{X}}|\boldsymbol{{\hat{X}}}) + {I}(\boldsymbol{{X}};\boldsymbol{{Y}})
nodes.label: eq:cv:etp

nodes.name: Entropy of X
Equation (36)
nodes.statement: {H}(\boldsymbol{{X}}) = \log \binom{n}{d}.
nodes.label: eq:cv:H(x)

nodes.name: Fano
Equation (37)
nodes.statement: {H}(\boldsymbol{{X}} | \boldsymbol{{\hat{X}}}) \le 1 + \varepsilon \log\binom{n}{d}.
nodes.label: eq:cv:H(x|xh)

nodes.name: Markov chain
Equation (38)
nodes.statement: (\boldsymbol{{X}}, {Y}^{i-1}) - {Z}_i - {Y}_i.
nodes.label: eq:markov:y_i:z_i

nodes.name: Mutual information bound
Equation (39)
nodes.statement:
I(\boldsymbol{{X}};\boldsymbol{{Y}})&=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{T} \left[{H}({Y}_i | {Y}^{i-1}) - {H}({Y}_i |\boldsymbol{{X}},{Y}^{i-1})\right] \notag\\
                                  &\leq \sum\limits_{i=1}^{T} \left[{H}({Y}_i  ) - {H}({Y}_i | \boldsymbol{{X}},{Y}^{i-1})\right]  \notag\\
                                  &\leq\sum\limits_{i=1}^{T} \left[{H}({Y}_i  ) - {H}({Y}_i | \boldsymbol{{X}},{Y}^{i-1},{Z}_i)\right] \notag\\
                                  &= \sum\limits_{i=1}^{T} \left[{H}({Y}_i  ) - {H}({Y}_i | {Z}_i)\right]
nodes.label: eq:cv:mi_3

nodes.name: Pool statistics
Equation (40)
nodes.statement: \Pr({Z}_i={a}) &= \frac{\binom{d}{{a}}\binom{n-d}{{\chi}_i-{a}}}{\binom{n}{{\chi}_i}}.

nodes.name: Equation (41)
nodes.label: eq:cv:def:p_miu_v

nodes.name: Lemma 10
Per-test mutual information bound
nodes.statement:
\begin{equation} {H}({Y}_i) - {H}({Y}_i | {Z}_i) \leq \frac{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}_i) \log e}{{\mu}({\chi}_i)(1-{\mu}({\chi}_i))}
\end{equation}
nodes.label: lem:cv_H

nodes.name: Pointer to the proof of Lemma 10
nodes.statement: See Appendix \ref{app:lem_cv}.

nodes.name: Optimize pool size
Equation (43)
nodes.statement:
{I}(\boldsymbol{{X}};\boldsymbol{{Y}}) 
    
    &\leq \sum\limits_{i=1}^{T} \frac{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}_i)\log e}{{\mu}({\chi}_i)(1-{\mu}({\chi}_i))} \notag\\
    
    &\leq T \times \frac{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^*) \log e}{{\mu}({\chi}^*)(1-{\mu}({\chi}^*))},
nodes.label: eq:cv:maxH_3

nodes.name: Equation (44)
nodes.statement: {\chi}^*:=\mathrm{argmax}_{{\chi}\in \{1,\dots,n-1\}} \frac{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi})}{{\mu}({\chi})(1-{\mu}({\chi}))}.
nodes.label: eq:cv:def:X*

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement_short: Combine to get the lower bound on $T$.

nodes.name: Equation (45)
nodes.statement: T \geq \frac{{\mu}({\chi}^*)\left(1-{\mu}({\chi}^*)\right)}{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^*) \log e} \left( (1-\varepsilon)\log\binom{n}{d} - 1 \right).
nodes.label: eq:cv:lower_bound

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Use Proposition 4's pair $(\hat L,\hat U)$ in the definition of $H(f)$ to bound the upper bound by $O(P_{\min}(q^*)d\log(n/\varepsilon)/\sigma^2(\chi^*))$ and compare with the converse.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: In this section, we argue that the upper bound in \eqref{eq:thm:T:ub} given by the proposed testing algorithm is at most a ${\cal O}\left( \frac{{P_{min}({{q}^*})}}{{\mu}({\chi}^{*}) \left( 1-{\mu}({\chi}^{*}) \right)} \right)$ factor larger than the lower bound in \eqref{eq:T:lower:bound}.

nodes.name: Recall definitions
Equation (46)
nodes.label: eq:rep:def:mu:v:chi

nodes.name: Define theta and eta
Equation (47)
nodes.statement: {\vartheta}&:={\chi}^{*}\frac{d}{n},
nodes.label: eq:def:vartheta

nodes.name: Equation (48)
nodes.label: eq:match:def:eta

nodes.name: Lemma 11
Existence of a steep point relative to theta
nodes.statement:
$\exists\,  {\kappa} \in \{0,1,\cdots,d-1,d\} \backslash \{{\eta}\}$ such that
\begin{equation} \left({\gamma}({\kappa}) \frac{f({\kappa}) - f({\eta})}{ {\kappa}-{\vartheta} } \right) ^2  > \frac{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^{*})}{11}, 
\end{equation}
 where ${\gamma}({\kappa}):=\min\left\{ |{\kappa}-{\vartheta}|, \sqrt{{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{{\vartheta}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\vartheta}+1} \right\}$.
nodes.label: lem:match

nodes.name: Equation (49)
nodes.statement: \left({\gamma}({\kappa}) \frac{f({\kappa}) - f({\eta})}{ {\kappa}-{\vartheta} } \right) ^2  > \frac{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^{*})}{11},
nodes.label: eq:mt:sttmt

nodes.name: Pointer to the proof of Lemma 11
nodes.statement: See Appendix \ref{app:lem_match}.

nodes.name: Proposition 4
Good pair (L-hat, U-hat) for H(f)
nodes.statement:
$\exists\, {\hat{L}},{\hat{U}} \in \{0,\dots,  d\}$ with ${\hat{L}}<{\hat{U}}$ such that 
\begin{equation} \left(  {\beta} \frac{f({\hat{U}})-f({\hat{L}})}{{\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}}} \right)^2 \geq \frac{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^{*})}{176},

\end{equation}
where ${\beta} := \min \left\{ {\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}} , \sqrt{{\hat{L}}+1} , \sqrt{d-{\hat{U}}+1} \right\}$ and ${\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^{*})$ is defined in \eqref{eq:rep:def:mu:v:chi}.
nodes.statement_short: Integers $\hat L<\hat U$ exist with $(\beta(f(\hat U)-f(\hat L))/(\hat U-\hat L))^2\ge\sigma^2(\chi^*)/176$.
nodes.label: prop:match

nodes.name: Equation (50)
nodes.statement: \left(  {\beta} \frac{f({\hat{U}})-f({\hat{L}})}{{\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}}} \right)^2 \geq \frac{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^{*})}{176},
nodes.label: eq:math:key-equation

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement_short: Set $\hat L,\hat U$ to $\min/\max\{\kappa,\eta\}$ and compare $\gamma(\kappa)$ with $2\beta$ by triangle inequalities.

nodes.name: Construct pair
Equation (51)
nodes.statement: {\hat{L}}:= \min\{ {\kappa},{\eta} \}, \quad  {\hat{U}} := \max\{ {\kappa},{\eta} \}.

nodes.name: Equation (52)
nodes.statement: |{\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}}|&=\left|{\kappa}-{\eta}\right| ,
nodes.label: eq:u-l=k-the

nodes.name: Equation (53)
nodes.statement: \sqrt{{\hat{L}}+1}&=\min\left\{ \sqrt{{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{{\eta}+1} \right\}   ,
nodes.label: eq:l:min:kthe

nodes.name: Equation (54)
nodes.statement: \sqrt{d-{\hat{U}}+1}&=\min\left\{\sqrt{d-{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\eta}+1}\right\} ,
nodes.label: eq:u:max:kthe

nodes.name: Equation (55)
nodes.statement: \left(f({\hat{U}})-f({\hat{L}})\right)^2&=\left(f({\kappa})-f\left({\eta}\right)\right)^2.
nodes.label: eq:fu-fl=fk-fo

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
Width comparison
Equation (56)
nodes.statement: 4({\kappa} - {\vartheta})^2 \ge 2({\kappa} - {\vartheta})^2 + 2({\vartheta} - {\eta})^2 \ge ({\kappa} -{\vartheta}+{\vartheta}- {\eta})^2 = ({\hat{U}} - {\hat{L}})^2.
nodes.label: eq:k-theta:u-l

nodes.name: Gamma vs beta
nodes.statement:
Recalling the definition of ${\gamma}({\kappa})$ in Lemma \ref{lem:match}, we have 
\begin{align} {\gamma}({\kappa}) &= \min\left\{ |{\kappa}-{\vartheta}|, \sqrt{{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{{\vartheta}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\vartheta}+1} \right\} \notag\\
    &\le \min\left\{ |{\kappa}-{\eta}| + |{\eta}-{\vartheta}|, \sqrt{{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{{\vartheta}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\vartheta}+1} \right\} \notag\\
    &\le \min\left\{ |{\kappa}-{\eta}| + 1, \sqrt{{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{{\eta}+2}, \sqrt{d-{\eta}+2} \right\} \notag\\
    &\le \min\left\{ 2|{\kappa}-{\eta}|, 2\sqrt{{\kappa}+1}, 2\sqrt{d-{\kappa}+1}, 2\sqrt{{\eta}+1}, 2\sqrt{d-{\eta}+1} \right\} \notag\\
    &= \min\left\{ 2|{\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}}|, 2\sqrt{{\hat{L}}+1}, 2\sqrt{d-{\hat{U}}+1} \right\} \notag\\
    &= 2 {\beta},  
\end{align}
where the second line follows from the triangle inequality $|{\kappa}-{\vartheta}|\leq |{\kappa}-{\eta}| + |{\eta}-{\vartheta}|$; the third line is because $|{\eta}-{\vartheta} |\leq 1$;









the fourth line follows from $|{\kappa}-{\eta}|\geq 1$;
the fifth line follows from \eqref{eq:u-l=k-the}, \eqref{eq:l:min:kthe} and \eqref{eq:u:max:kthe}.

nodes.name: Equation (57)
nodes.statement:
{\gamma}({\kappa}) &= \min\left\{ |{\kappa}-{\vartheta}|, \sqrt{{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{{\vartheta}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\vartheta}+1} \right\} \notag\\
    &\le \min\left\{ |{\kappa}-{\eta}| + |{\eta}-{\vartheta}|, \sqrt{{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{{\vartheta}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\vartheta}+1} \right\} \notag\\
    &\le \min\left\{ |{\kappa}-{\eta}| + 1, \sqrt{{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{d-{\kappa}+1}, \sqrt{{\eta}+2}, \sqrt{d-{\eta}+2} \right\} \notag\\
    &\le \min\left\{ 2|{\kappa}-{\eta}|, 2\sqrt{{\kappa}+1}, 2\sqrt{d-{\kappa}+1}, 2\sqrt{{\eta}+1}, 2\sqrt{d-{\eta}+1} \right\} \notag\\
    &= \min\left\{ 2|{\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}}|, 2\sqrt{{\hat{L}}+1}, 2\sqrt{d-{\hat{U}}+1} \right\} \notag\\
    &= 2 {\beta},
nodes.label: ineq:gama:beta

nodes.name: Conclusion
Equation (58)
nodes.statement: \left(  {\beta} \frac{f({\hat{U}})-f({\hat{L}})}{{\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}}} \right)^2 \geq \frac {{\gamma}({\kappa})^2}{4} \times\frac{(f({\kappa})-f({\eta}))^2}{4({\kappa}-{\vartheta})^2} > \frac{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^{*})}{176}.

nodes.name: Upper bound via Proposition 4
nodes.statement:
Now we set out to prove Theorem \ref{thm:match}. Recalling the upper bound on $T$ in \eqref{eq:thm:T:ub}, we have
\begin{align*}
     T &\leq 376017  {P_{min}({{q}^*})}  {H(f)} d\log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon } \right)+1 \\
       &\leq  376017  {P_{min}({{q}^*})} \left(\frac{1}{\min\left\{{\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}} , \sqrt{{\hat{L}}+1} , \sqrt{d-{\hat{U}}+1}\right\}}\times \frac{{\hat{U}}-{\hat{L}}}{f({\hat{U}})-f({\hat{L}})} \right)^2 d\log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon } \right)+1\\
       &\leq  376017  {P_{min}({{q}^*})} \frac{176}{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^*)} d\log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon } \right)+1
\end{align*}
where the second inequality follows from the definition of ${H(f)}$ in \eqref{eq:def:sensi:para} by letting $({L},{U})$ therein to be the pair $({\hat{L}},{\hat{U}})$ in Proposition \ref{prop:match}; the last inequality follows from Proposition \ref{prop:match}. This implies that the upper bound in \eqref{eq:thm:T:ub} scales as 

${\cal O} \left( \frac{{P_{min}({{q}^*})}}{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^*)} d \log \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon} \right) \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Plug $(\hat L,\hat U)$ into $H(f)$ and apply Proposition 4.

nodes.name: Compare with converse
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by the definition of ${h(f)}$ in \eqref{eq:def:concen:para}, the lower bound in \eqref{eq:T:lower:bound} scales as $\Omega\left(\frac{{\mu}({\chi}^*)\left(1-{\mu}({\chi}^*)\right)}{{\sigma^{2}}({\chi}^*)}\log \binom{n}{d}\right)$. By standard arguments via Stirling’s approximation, $\log \binom{n}{d}$ is at least $d \log \frac n d$. Thus, under the assumptions that $d=n^\theta, 0\leq\theta< 1$, the number of tests $T$ required for $(1-\varepsilon)$-reliable recovery in Theorem \ref{thm:main} is up to a ${\cal O}\left( \frac{{P_{min}({{q}^*})}}{{\mu}({\chi}^{*}) \left( 1-{\mu}({\chi}^{*}) \right)} \right)$ factor larger than the lower bound presented in Theorem \ref{thm:converse}.
nodes.statement_short: Compare with the converse to get the ratio.

nodes.name: Universal gap
nodes.statement: From Remarks \ref{remark:ub} and \ref{remark:lb}, we know that our upper and lower bounds scale as ${\cal O}\left(d^{2+o(1)}\log n\right)$ and $\Omega\left(d\log n\right)$, respectively. Therefore, the number of tests required in Theorem \ref{thm:main} is never more than a ${\cal O}(d^{1+o(1)})$ factor larger than the information-theoretic lower bound in Theorem \ref{thm:converse}.

nodes.name: Simulation procedure
nodes.statement_short: Monte Carlo evaluation: random defective set, Bernoulli test matrix, noisy outcomes via $f$, decode and check exact recovery.

nodes.name: Generate X
nodes.statement: For given $(n,d,f,T)$, we randomly generate an array $\boldsymbol{X}$ of length $n$ with $(n-d)$ 0s and $d$ 1s, where 0 represents non-defective and 1 represents defective.
nodes.statement_short: Draw a random defective vector $X$ of weight $d$.

nodes.name: Generate M
nodes.statement: Then we choose the parameter ${q}$ accordingly, and randomly generate a $T\times n$ matrix $\boldsymbol{M}$ where each entry is i.i.d. Bernoulli(${q}$).
nodes.statement_short: Choose $q$ and draw the Bernoulli test matrix $M$.

nodes.name: Generate outcomes
nodes.statement: Finally, we compute $\boldsymbol{Z} =(Z_1,\dots,Z_T)=  \boldsymbol{M}  \boldsymbol{X} $ and generate the test outcomes according to $f(Z_i), i=1,\dots, T$.

nodes.name: Decode
nodes.statement: Depending on the value of ${q}$, we then use the decoding rules \eqref{eq:classification_small_q} or \eqref{eq:classification_large_q}.

nodes.name: Check success
nodes.statement: Let $\boldsymbol{\hat{X}}$ be the estimation of the decoder. The test succeeds if $\boldsymbol{\hat{X}} = \boldsymbol{X}$, and fails otherwise.

nodes.name: Simulation of the threshold test function
nodes.section: 9.1 Simulation result for threshold test function in Corollary 1-coro_threshold
nodes.statement_short: Threshold $f$ with $\ell=5$: success probability exceeds 0.99 once $T\gtrsim 17$-$20\,d\log n$.

nodes.section: 9.1 Simulation result for threshold test function in Corollary 1-coro_threshold
nodes.label: eq:threshold_L=5

nodes.name: Simulation of the linear test function
nodes.statement: We now consider the function $f(\cdot)$ defined in \eqref{eq:linear:function} and illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:f:case2}. In Corollary \ref{coro:special:cases}-\ref{coro_linear}, we have shown that our algorithm is order-wise optimal and the number of tests $T$ scales as $\Theta (d^2 \log n)$. For ease of implementation, we assign ${q} = \frac{1}{2}$. In the waterfall plot in Figure \ref{sim:fig:waterfall_linear}, $n=2000$, $d=20$, the $x$-axis plots the number of tests $T$ ranging from $  T_{min} '= 0$ to $T_{max} '= \left\lfloor 40d^2 \log n  \right\rfloor$ with step size $\Delta_T' = \left\lfloor \frac{T_{max} - T_{min}}{100} \right\rfloor$, and the $y$-axis plots the probability of successful reconstruction calculated by $100$ trials for each test $ T = T_{min}' + j \times \Delta_T' , j \in \{0,1,\dots,100\}$. When $T \gtrapprox  21.6  d^2 \log n$, the probability of successful reconstruction exceeds $0.99$. In the heat-map figure \ref{sim:fig:heatmap_linear_d}, $n=2000$, the $x$-axis denotes the number of defectives $d$ ranging from $20$ to $70$, and the $y$-axis denotes the number of tests $T$ as a multiple of $d^2\log n $. In the heat-map figure \ref{sim:fig:heatmap_linear_n}, $d=20$, the $x$-axis corresponds to the number of items $n$ ranging from $2000$ to $4000$, and the $y$-axis corresponds to the number of tests $T$ as a multiple of $d^2\log n $. In both figures \ref{sim:fig:heatmap_linear_d} and \ref{sim:fig:heatmap_linear_n}, each pixel is coloured according to the probability of successful reconstruction calculated by $100$ trials for each test $T$-- the lighter the colour, the higher the probability of reconstruction success. For each value of $d$ (respectively $n$) in figure \ref{sim:fig:heatmap_linear_d} (respectively figure \ref{sim:fig:heatmap_linear_n}), the corresponding red dot in that column represents the number of tests for which this probability first equals $0.99$. The horizontal blue dashed line indicates that when $T \gtrapprox 20.0d^2\log n $ (respectively $19.6d^2\log n $), the probability of successful reconstruction generally exceeds $0.99$.
nodes.section: 9.2 Simulation result for linear test function in Corollary 1-coro_linear
nodes.statement_short: Linear $f$: success probability exceeds 0.99 once $T\gtrsim 20\,d^2\log n$.

nodes.name: Simulations supporting Conjecture 1
nodes.statement_short: For a partial-linear and a sigmoid $f$, $\min_q\Gamma(q)/(h(f)d\log n)\le2$.

nodes.name: Equation (60)

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement_short: Expand $P$ and $Q$ with Pascal's rule to write $\Delta$ and $\nabla$ as binomially weighted increments of $f$; monotonicity gives the inequalities.

nodes.name: Expand P(-,q)
nodes.statement:
We expand ${P(-,{q})}, {P(+,{q})},{Q(-,{q})}$ and ${P(+,{q})}$ using elementary combinatorial and algebraic identities. 
Regarding ${P(-,{q})}$, we have that 
\begin{align} {P(-,{q})} &= \sum\limits_{j=0}^{d} \binom{d}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j) \notag\\ 
  &= (1-{q})^d f(0)+ \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d-1} \binom{d}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j) +{q}^d f(d) \notag\\ 
 &=(1-{q})^d f(0)+ \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d-1} \left( \binom{d-1}{j} + \binom{d-1}{j-1} \right) {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j)  +{q}^d f(d) \notag\\ 
&= \sum\limits_{j=0}^{d-1} \binom{d-1}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j) + \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d} \binom{d-1}{j-1} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j).
\end{align}

nodes.name: Equation (77)
nodes.statement:
{P(-,{q})} &= \sum\limits_{j=0}^{d} \binom{d}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j) \notag\\ 
  &= (1-{q})^d f(0)+ \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d-1} \binom{d}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j) +{q}^d f(d) \notag\\ 
 &=(1-{q})^d f(0)+ \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d-1} \left( \binom{d-1}{j} + \binom{d-1}{j-1} \right) {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j)  +{q}^d f(d) \notag\\ 
&= \sum\limits_{j=0}^{d-1} \binom{d-1}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j) + \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d} \binom{d-1}{j-1} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j).
nodes.label: eq:convert_p-

nodes.name: Formula for nabla
nodes.statement:
Similarly, regarding ${Q(-,{q})}$, we have
\begin{align*}
    {Q(-,{q})} &= \sum\limits_{j=0}^{d} \binom{d}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j) \\ 
    &= \sum\limits_{j=0}^{d-1} \binom{d-1}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j) + \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d} \binom{d-1}{j-1} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j).
\end{align*}
And regarding ${Q(+,{q})}$, we have
\begin{align*}
    {Q(+,{q})} &= \sum\limits_{j=0}^{d-1} \binom{d-1}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-1-j} f(j) \\ 
    &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d} \binom{d-1}{j-1} {q}^{j-1} (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j-1) \\ 
    &= (1-{q}) \sum\limits_{j=0}^{d-1} \binom{d-1}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-1-j} f(j) + {q} \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d} \binom{d-1}{j-1} {q}^{j-1} (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j-1) \\
    &= \sum\limits_{j=0}^{d-1} \binom{d-1}{j} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j) + \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d} \binom{d-1}{j-1} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} f(j-1).
\end{align*}
It then follows that 
\begin{align} {\nabla({q})} &={Q(-,{q})}-{Q(+,{q})} \\
    & =\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d} \binom{d-1}{j-1} {q}^j (1-{q})^{d-j} (f(j)-f(j-1)) \notag \\ 
    &= \sum\limits_{j=0}^{d-1} \binom{d-1}{j} {q}^{j+1} (1-{q})^{d-j-1} (f(j+1)-f(j)) \notag\\ 
    &= \frac{{q}}{1-{q}} {\Delta({q})},

\end{align}
where the last equality follows from \eqref{eq:convert_delta}. This together with \eqref{eq:P+>=P-} implies that 
\begin{align} {\nabla({q})} > 0 \; \text {  or equivalently  }\;  {Q(-,{q})} >  {Q(+,{q})}.
\end{align}

Union bound
Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement:
To begin with, assume that each item participates in at least ${m}$ tests, i.e., ${{m}_{i}} \ge {m}$ for all items $i$. As discussed in Decoding Rule $1$, we identify item $i$ via (\ref{eq:classification_small_q}). Two types of error can happen:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Item $i$ is non-defective, but is identified as defective, i.e., false alarm;
\item Item $i$ is defective, but is identified as non-defective, i.e., missed detection.
\end{enumerate}
We will bound the probabilities of $1)$ and $2)$ occuring separately as follows. For notational simplicity, let ${\rho} = {P(-,{q})}$, ${\nu} = {P(+,{q})}$, ${\Delta} = {\Delta({q})}$, ${P_{\min}} = {P_{\min}({q})}$. Recall that by Definition \ref{item:def:Delta}, ${\Delta}={\nu}-{\rho}$. 

\subsubsection{\underline{False alarm for item $i$}} 
In this scenario, each test outcome is positive with probability ${\rho}$, and
\begin{equation}
    \frac{{{m}_{i}^+}}{{{m}_{i}}} > \frac{{\rho}+{\nu}}{2}.
\end{equation}
Let ${P_{\text{FA}}}$ denote the probability of this false alarm. Since the test outcomes are independent due to the tests being constructed in an i.i.d. manner, ${{m}_{i}^+} \sim \text{Binomial}({{m}_{i}},{\rho})$. From Fact~\ref{chernoff_bound}, ${P_{\text{FA}}}$ can be bounded as
\begin{align} {P_{\text{FA}}} &= \Pr \left( \frac{{{m}_{i}^+}}{{{m}_{i}}} > \frac{{\rho}+{\nu}}{2} \right) \notag\\
&= \Pr \left( {{m}_{i}^+} > \left( 1+\frac{{\Delta}}{2{\rho}} \right) {\rho} {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&\le \exp\left( - \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{{\Delta}^2}{4{\rho}^2} \times {\rho} {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&= \exp \left( -\frac{{\Delta}^2}{12{\rho}} {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\
&\le \exp \left( -\frac{{\Delta}^2}{12{\rho}} {m} \right).
\end{align}
On the other hand, we also have ${{m}_{i}^-} \sim \text{Binomial} ({{m}_{i}},1-{\rho})$. From Fact~\ref{chernoff_bound}, ${P_{\text{FA}}}$ can also be bounded as
\begin{align} {P_{\text{FA}}} &= \Pr \left( \frac{{{m}_{i}^+}}{{{m}_{i}}} > \frac{{\rho}+{\nu}}{2} \right) \notag\\
&= \Pr \left( \frac{{{m}_{i}^-}}{{{m}_{i}}} < 1 - \frac{{\rho}+{\nu}}{2} \right) \notag\\ 
&= \Pr \left( {{m}_{i}^-} < \left( 1 - \frac{{\Delta}}{2(1-{\rho})} \right) (1 - {\rho}) {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&\le \exp\left( - \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{{\Delta}^2}{4(1-{\rho})^2} (1 - {\rho}) {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&= \exp \left( - \frac{{\Delta}^2}{12(1-{\rho})} {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\
&\le \exp \left( - \frac{{\Delta}^2}{12(1-{\rho})} {m} \right).
\end{align}
Combining \eqref{eq:false_defective_1} and \eqref{eq:false_defective_2}, we obtain
\begin{align} {P_{\text{FA}}} &\leq \exp\left( -\frac{{\Delta}^2}{12\min\{{\rho},1-{\rho}\}}{m} \right) \notag\\
   &\leq \exp\left( - \frac{{\Delta}^2}{12{P_{\min}}} {m} \right)  \notag\\
   &\leq \frac{\varepsilon}{2n},
\end{align}

where the second inequality follows from \eqref{eq:def:Pmin} and \eqref{ineq:relation:P:Q}; the last inequality follows by substituting the definition of ${m}$ in \eqref{eq:def:m}.  
\subsubsection{\underline{Missed detection for item $i$}} The calculations are similar to those above analyzing the probability of a false alarm for item $i$. In this case, each test outcome is positive with probability ${\nu}$, and
\begin{equation}
    \frac{{{m}_{i}^+}}{{{m}_{i}}} \le \frac{{\rho}+{\nu}}{2}.
\end{equation}
Let ${P_{\text{MD}}}$ denote the probability of this false non-defective. Again since the test outcomes are independent, we have ${{m}_{i}^+} \sim \text{Binomial}({{m}_{i}},{\nu})$. From Fact~\ref{chernoff_bound}, we can bound ${P_{\text{MD}}}$ as
\begin{align} {P_{\text{MD}}} &= \Pr \left( \frac{{{m}_{i}^+}}{{{m}_{i}}} \le \frac{{\rho}+{\nu}}{2} \right) \notag\\
&= \Pr \left( {{m}_{i}^+} \le \left( 1-\frac{{\Delta}}{2{\nu}} \right) {\nu} {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&\le \exp\left( - \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{{\Delta}^2}{4{\nu}^2} \times {\nu} {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&= \exp \left( -\frac{{\Delta}^2}{12{\nu}} {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\
&\le \exp \left( -\frac{{\Delta}^2}{12{\nu}} {m} \right).
\end{align}
From another perspective, ${{m}_{i}^-} \sim \text{Binomial} ({{m}_{i}},1-{\nu})$. From Fact~\ref{chernoff_bound}, we can also bound ${P_{\text{MD}}}$ as
\begin{align} {P_{\text{MD}}} &= \Pr \left( \frac{{{m}_{i}^+}}{{{m}_{i}}} \le \frac{{\rho}+{\nu}}{2} \right) \notag\\
&= \Pr \left( \frac{{{m}_{i}^-}}{{{m}_{i}}} \ge 1 - \frac{{\rho}+{\nu}}{2} \right) \notag\\ 
&= \Pr \left( {{m}_{i}^-} \ge \left( 1 + \frac{{\Delta}}{2(1-{\nu})} \right) (1 - {\nu}) {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&\le \exp\left( - \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{{\Delta}^2}{4(1-{\nu})^2} (1 - {\nu}) {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&= \exp \left( - \frac{{\Delta}^2}{12(1-{\nu})} {{m}_{i}} \right) \notag\\
&\le \exp \left( - \frac{{\Delta}^2}{12(1-{\nu})} {m} \right).
\end{align}
Combining \eqref{eq:false_non_defective_1} and \eqref{eq:false_non_defective_2}, we see that
\begin{align} {P_{\text{MD}}} &\leq \exp\left( -\frac{{\Delta}^2}{12 \min\{{\nu},1-{\nu}\}} {m} \right) \notag\\
    &\leq \exp\left( - \frac{{\Delta}^2}{12{P_{\min}}} {m} \right) \notag\\
    &\leq \frac{\varepsilon}{2n},
\end{align}
where the second inequality follows from \eqref{eq:def:Pmin} and \eqref{ineq:relation:P:Q}; the last inequality follows from the definition of ${m}$ in \eqref{eq:def:m}.



From \eqref{eq:false_defective} and \eqref{eq:false_non_defective} we conclude that for any item $i\in\mathcal{N}$, the probability of  misidentification (either false alarm or missed detection) is smaller than $\frac{\varepsilon}{2n}$. Therefore, when all items participate in at least ${m}$ tests, by the union bound the probability that all items are correctly identified is bounded from below by
\begin{equation}
    1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{2n} \times n = 1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{2},
\end{equation}
which concludes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:num_tests_correctness}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement:
Recall that in \eqref{eq:T_large_q}, $T$ was chosen to satisfy $T \ge \frac{13}{6(1-{q})} {s}$. 
Consider an arbitrary item $i\in {\cal N}$. 

Since each item does not participate in a test i.i.d. with probability $1-{q}$,  
the expected number of tests without item $i$ is
\begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}({{s}_{i}}) &= (1-{q}) T \notag \\ 
    &\ge \frac{13}{6} {s} \notag \\ 
    &= 2{s} + \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{12{P_{\min}({q})}}{({\nabla({q})})^2} \ln \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon} \right) \notag\\
    &\ge 2{s} + 2\ln \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon} \right), \end{align}
where the third line follows from the definition of ${s}$ in \eqref{eq:def:mo}; the last line follows from \eqref{eq:1>=pmin>max:Delta}.



Let ${\hat{\mathcal{E}}}_i$ be the event that item $i$ participates in more than $T-{s}$.  In other words, the number of tests without item $i$ is less than ${s}$. By Fact~\ref{chernoff_bound}, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \Pr ({\hat{\mathcal{E}}}_i)&= \Pr \left({{s}_{i}} < {s} = \left( 1 - \frac{ \mathbb{E}({{s}_{i}})-{s}}{ \mathbb{E}({{s}_{i}})} \right)  \mathbb{E}({{s}_{i}}) \right) \\
    &\leq \exp \left( - \left( \frac{ \mathbb{E}({{s}_{i}})-{s}}{ \mathbb{E}({{s}_{i}})} \right)^2 \, \frac{ \mathbb{E}({{s}_{i}})}{2} \right) \\
    &= \exp \left( - \frac{ \mathbb{E}({{s}_{i}})}{2} + {s} - \frac{{s}^2}{2 \mathbb{E}({{s}_{i}})} \right) \\
    &\leq \exp \left( -\frac{ \mathbb{E}({{s}_{i}})}{2} + {s} \right) \\
    &\leq \exp \left( -\ln \left( \frac{2n}{\varepsilon} \right) \right)
    = \frac{\varepsilon}{2n},
    \end{align*} 
    where the last inequality follows from \eqref{eq:l:ETi_4}.
By the union bound, the probability that each item participates in at most $T-{s}$ tests can be bounded from below by
\begin{equation}
    1 - \Pr\left( \bigcup\limits_{i}{\hat{\mathcal{E}}}_i \right) \ge 1 - \sum\limits_i \Pr({\hat{\mathcal{E}}}_i) > 1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{2n} \times n = 1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff lower-tail bound on the number of tests excluding an item, then a union bound.

nodes.statement_short: Same as Lemma 5 for tests excluding the item: two Chernoff bounds per error type, $P_{\min}$, definition of $s$, union bound.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: To begin with, assume that each item participates in at most $T-{s}$ tests, i.e., ${{s}_{i}} \ge {s}$ for all items $i$. As discussed in Decoding Rule $2$, we identify item $i$ via (\ref{eq:classification_large_q}). Two types of error can happen:

nodes.name: Error type 1
nodes.statement: Item $i$ is non-defective, but is identified as defective, i.e., false alarm;

nodes.name: Error type 2
nodes.statement: Item $i$ is defective, but is identified as non-defective, i.e., missed detection.

nodes.name: Notation
False alarm
nodes.statement:
In this scenario, each test outcome is positive with probability ${\hat{{\rho}}}$, and
\begin{equation}
    \frac{{{s}_{i}^+}}{{{s}_{i}}} \le \frac{{\hat{{\rho}}}+{\hat{{\nu}}}}{2}.
\end{equation}
Let ${\hat{P}_{\text{FA}}}$ denote the probability of this false alarm. Since the test outcomes are independent due to the tests being constructed in an i.i.d. manner, ${{s}_{i}^+} \sim \text{Binomial}({{s}_{i}},{\hat{{\rho}}})$. From Fact~\ref{chernoff_bound}, ${\hat{P}_{\text{FA}}}$ can be bounded as
\begin{align} {\hat{P}_{\text{FA}}} &= \Pr \left( \frac{{{s}_{i}^+}}{{{s}_{i}}} \le \frac{{\hat{{\rho}}}+{\hat{{\nu}}}}{2} \right) \notag\\
&= \Pr \left( {{s}_{i}^+} \le \left( 1-\frac{{\nabla}}{2{\hat{{\rho}}}} \right) {\hat{{\rho}}} {{s}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&\le \exp\left( - \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{{\nabla}^2}{4{\hat{{\rho}}}^2} \times {\hat{{\rho}}} {{s}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&= \exp \left( -\frac{{\nabla}^2}{12{\hat{{\rho}}}} {{s}_{i}} \right) \notag\\
&\le \exp \left( -\frac{{\nabla}^2}{12{\hat{{\rho}}}} {s} \right).
\end{align}
On the other hand, we also have ${{s}_{i}^-} \sim \text{Binomial} ({{s}_{i}},1-{\hat{{\rho}}})$. From Fact~\ref{chernoff_bound}, ${\hat{P}_{\text{FA}}}$ can also be bounded as

\begin{align} {\hat{P}_{\text{FA}}} &= \Pr \left( \frac{{{s}_{i}^+}}{{{s}_{i}}} \le \frac{{\hat{{\rho}}}+{\hat{{\nu}}}}{2} \right) \notag\\
&= \Pr \left( \frac{{{s}_{i}^-}}{{{s}_{i}}} \ge 1 - \frac{{\hat{{\rho}}}+{\hat{{\nu}}}}{2} \right) \notag\\ 
&= \Pr \left( {{s}_{i}^-} \ge \left( 1 + \frac{{\nabla}}{2(1-{\hat{{\rho}}})} \right) (1 - {\hat{{\rho}}}) {{s}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&\le \exp\left( - \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{{\nabla}^2}{4(1-{\hat{{\rho}}})^2} (1 - {\hat{{\rho}}}) {{s}_{i}} \right) \notag\\ 
&= \exp \left( - \frac{{\nabla}^2}{12(1-{\hat{{\rho}}})} {{s}_{i}} \right) \notag\\
&\le \exp \left( - \frac{{\nabla}^2}{12(1-{\hat{{\rho}}})} {s} \right).
\end{align}
Combining \eqref{eq:false_defective_1_l} and \eqref{eq:false_defective_2_l}, we obtain
\begin{equation} {\hat{P}_{\text{FA}}} \le \exp\left( -\frac{{\nabla}^2}{12 \min\{{\hat{{\rho}}}, 1-{\hat{{\rho}}}\}} {s} \right) \le \exp\left( - \frac{{\nabla}^2}{12{P_{\min}}} {s} \right) \le \frac{\varepsilon}{2n},
\end{equation}

where the second inequality follows from \eqref{eq:def:Pmin} and \eqref{ineq:relation:P:Q}; the last inequality follows by substituting the definition of ${s}$ in \eqref{eq:def:mo}.
